# Purpose and review status

This document adapts the existing YFB model in multiomicsGEP to matched
expression and DNA methylation measurements. It is a methodological proposal
for advisor review, not a report of a fitted multimodal model. No production
fitting code, model defaults, simulations, or real-data analyses are changed.

There are two distinct adaptations to assess. First, partition the features
by modality and estimate separate loading priors while sharing the subject
scores. Second, derive the survival-feedback version of YFB from a coherent
objective. The current default YFB algorithm suppresses survival feedback
into the loadings. Its direct multimodal counterpart is retained here as a
compatibility baseline. Differences required by a joint derivation are
identified separately from differences required simply by adding a modality.

The intended application has **one training cohort** and **one independent
validation cohort**, each with matched expression and methylation data.
The validation subjects are not additional training subjects. One
right-censored survival endpoint is assumed. Outcome-dependent decisions
must use training data only.

The starting prior is nonnegative point-exponential for both $L$ and each
$F_m$, with separate fitted parameters for every column and modality.
Signed alternatives are derived for comparison. All $K$ score columns are
shared, but an entire loading column may vanish in one modality. Ordinary
observation likelihood is examined first; explicit modality weighting is
an alternative, not an assumed solution.

**Choices still requiring advisor review:** loading support and analysis
scale; ordinary versus weighted objective; raw versus normalized survival
projection; and the approximation used for joint inference. The derivations
below make those choices reviewable without claiming they have been selected.

# Current implementation: the reference to be adapted

The source audit refers to repository revision c13eaea, inspected on
September 10, 2026. The executable modules take precedence over older
companion documents when identifying implemented behavior.

| Quantity | R representation | Implemented YFB behavior |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Subject scores | EL, EL2 | $n\times K$ means and second moments; omics-only update |
| Feature loadings | EF, EF2 | $p\times K$ means and second moments |
| Survival coefficients | EBeta, EBeta2 | $K$ means and second moments for a single cohort |
| Residual precision | Tau | $p$ point estimates, not a variational distribution |
| Projection scale | EF_norms | Training loading-column norms used for prediction |
| Priors | prior_LF, prior_beta | Defaults: point-exponential and Normal, respectively |

The relevant entry point is \path{code/fit_cox_on_yf.R}.
Its update modules are \path{code/update_L_surv_YFB.R},
\path{code/update_F_surv_YFB.R}, \path{code/update_beta.R}, and
\path{code/update_tau.R}. Prediction is in
\path{code/predict_cox_on_yf.R}.
For reference, the LB model in \path{code/fit_modular.R} uses $\eta=L\beta$,
whereas YFB predicts survival from projections of the observed omics.

The current YFB fit uses
$$
\widehat Z=Y\bar F D^{-1},\qquad
D_{kk}=\sqrt{\sum_j\bar f_{jk}^{\,2}+10^{-10}},\qquad
\widehat\eta=\widehat Z\bar\beta.
$$ {#eq-current-projection}

Here $Z$ is not $L$. Even with perfect reconstruction,
$YF=LF^\top F$ need not equal $L$.

The defaults are alpha_F = 0, alpha = 0.5, and boost_beta = FALSE.
Thus $L$ and $F$ use unweighted omics information, while the coefficient
update uses alpha times the survival quadratic. Fitting one prior per
column is already the pattern; the multimodal change is to fit one
loading prior per **modality and column**, instead of pooling all features
into that column's prior.

## Differences that a joint derivation must not conceal

1. **Feedback:** a Cox factor depending on $F$ contributes to its update.
   Setting alpha_F to zero removes that contribution. The resulting
   procedure is modular; it is not coordinate ascent on the full joint
   posterior specified below.
2. **Projection uncertainty:** passing $\widehat Z^2$ as a second moment
   treats the current estimated projection as fixed. Joint inference on
   $F$ requires additional variance terms.
3. **Feature interactions:** the existing optional survival contribution
   in update_F_surv_YFB.R uses only the diagonal of $Y^\top W Y$ and a
   factor-excluded working response. An exact scalar loading update also
   subtracts the contributions of the other features in that same factor.
4. **Curvature:** the helper calc_cox_taylor_yf computes a working curvature
   described precisely in Section @sec-cox. It is not the exact negative
   diagonal Hessian despite that wording in older comments.
5. **Objective weights:** under the default per_p reporting convention,
   the reported survival contribution is multiplied by $p$, while the
   coefficient update is not. Omics updates also do not use the reported
   factor $(1-\alpha)$. Therefore the reported combined diagnostic is not
   a single objective whose coordinate updates reproduce all defaults.
6. **Normalization:** the optional survival loading update is written for
   a linear, unnormalized projection; differentiating a normalized
   projection requires additional terms.

These observations motivate explicit comparisons. They are not changes to
the established single-modality implementation.

# Data, parameterization, and priors

## Matched blocks and notation

For modality $m\in\{1,\ldots,M\}$, let $Y_m\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_m}$.
Initially $M=2$: expression and methylation. Row $i$ refers to the same
subject in every block. Each subject has observed follow-up
$t_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and event indicator $\delta_i=1\{T_i\leq C_i\}$.
The likelihood below conditions on the realized preprocessing and feature
selection; fitting those operations is a separate training-only step.

$$
\begin{aligned}
p&=\sum_{m=1}^M p_m,&
Y&=[Y_1\ \cdots\ Y_M]\in\mathbb R^{n\times p},\\
F&=[F_1^\top\ \cdots\ F_M^\top]^\top\in\mathbb R^{p\times K},&
L&\in\mathbb R^{n\times K}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-blocks}

Use $k$ for a factor, $j$ for a feature within modality $m$, and $a=(m,j)$
for a flattened feature index. Gene and CpG identifiers occupy distinct
namespaces. No gene-to-CpG pairing is required.

The Gaussian observation model is
$$
y_{mij}\mid L,F_m,\tau_{mj}
\ \overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\
\Normal\left(\sum_{k=1}^K l_{ik}f_{mjk},\tau_{mj}^{-1}\right).
$$ {#eq-observation}

Conditional residual independence across features and modalities is an
assumption, not an assertion that CpGs are marginally independent.
Shared factors induce marginal dependence. Residual dependence left after
factorization is a potential source of overconfidence at large $p_m$.
Residual precisions vary across features within each modality. A single
modality-wide precision is not introduced.

For derivation of the linear YFB case, define **fixed** projection
coefficients $c_m$ and the columns
$$
x_{mj}=c_mY_m[:,j],\qquad
X=[c_1Y_1\ \cdots\ c_MY_M],\qquad
z_k=Xf_k,\qquad \eta=\sum_k\beta_k z_k.
$$ {#eq-projection}

The unweighted stacked projection has $c_m=1$ and
$Z=YF=\sum_mY_mF_m$. Coefficients $c_m$ change prediction, whereas the
likelihood weights introduced later change estimation of the reconstruction.
They are separate choices. In the core derivation they are fixed constants,
not parameters silently re-estimated at each iteration.

## Score and loading priors

Use conditionally independent entries with column-specific distributions:
$$
l_{ik}\sim g_{L_k},\qquad
f_{mjk}\sim g_{F_{mk}},\qquad
\beta_k\sim g_{\beta_k}.
$$ {#eq-priors}

The starting score and loading families are
$$
\begin{aligned}
g_{L_k}&=(1-\pi_{Lk})\delta_0+
          \pi_{Lk}\operatorname{Exp}(r_{Lk}),\\
g_{F_{mk}}&=(1-\pi_{Fmk})\delta_0+
          \pi_{Fmk}\operatorname{Exp}(r_{Fmk}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pe-prior}

Here $\pi$ is the **probability of the nonzero component**, $r>0$ is an
exponential rate, and $\delta_0$ is a unit point mass at zero. The package
scale parameter is $1/r$, not $r$. The prior mode remains fixed at zero.
There are $2K$ score-prior hyperparameters and $2MK$ loading-prior
hyperparameters before considering boundary cases. No additional
hyperpriors are imposed: these are empirical-Bayes estimates.

The minimal signed comparison replaces $g_{F_{mk}}$ by
$$
g_{F_{mk}}=(1-\pi_{Fmk})\delta_0+
             \pi_{Fmk}\Normal(0,s_{Fmk}^2).
$$ {#eq-pn-prior}

It can be applied to both modalities or to a prespecified subset.
The score family can remain point-exponential for that comparison. A
fully signed alternative also replaces $g_{L_k}$ by point-normal; this
is a separate modeling choice, particularly relevant for centered data.
The updates below support either family.

The coefficient baseline retains the implemented zero-centered Normal
family:
$$
\beta_k\sim\Normal(0,s_{\beta k}^2).
$$ {#eq-beta-prior}

Each variance is fitted empirically. With only one coefficient per factor,
this is a weakly informed, boundary-prone empirical-Bayes problem; it is
not pooling across $K$ coefficients. A common variance or spike-and-slab
coefficient family would be an additional choice, not a hidden default.
The document gives the Normal and spike-and-slab algebra so that such a
comparison is possible.

## What shared means

Sharing means the same $l_{ik}$ participates in every modality's
reconstruction. It does not require $\pi_{Fmk}>0$ or a nonzero posterior
column in every modality. A zero block in methylation leaves an
expression-only factor within the common $K$-column space.
Separate priors do not introduce different subject scores for each modality,
and no cross-modality prior ties $f_{1jk}$ to a particular CpG loading.

# From joint likelihood to the variational objective

## Observation and survival likelihoods

The complete Gaussian observation log-likelihood is
$$
\ell_m=
-\frac{np_m}{2}\log(2\pi)
+\frac n2\sum_j\log\tau_{mj}
-\frac12\sum_{i,j}\tau_{mj}
 \left(y_{mij}-\sum_kl_{ik}f_{mjk}\right)^2.
$$ {#eq-omics-likelihood}

Under proportional hazards, $h_i(t)=h_0(t)\exp(\eta_i)$.
Conditional on independent, noninformative censoring, the event-time
likelihood contribution, omitting censoring factors, is
$$
\mathcal L_T(h_0,\eta)=
\prod_i \{h_0(t_i)e^{\eta_i}\}^{\delta_i}
          \exp\{-H_0(t_i)e^{\eta_i}\}.
$$ {#eq-full-survival}

Consequently, a full joint likelihood with a specified baseline is
$\{\prod_m p(Y_m\mid L,F_m,\tau_m)\}\mathcal L_T(h_0,\eta)$.
Multiplying by the priors gives the corresponding posterior kernel.
This factorization is coherent even though $Y$ also enters $\eta$:
it specifies $p(Y\mid L,F,\tau)p(T\mid Y,F,\beta,h_0)$.

The existing method eliminates the baseline hazard from coefficient
estimation using the Cox partial likelihood. At distinct event time $u_r$,
write $\mathcal D_r=\{i:t_i=u_r,\delta_i=1\}$,
$d_r=|\mathcal D_r|$, and $\mathcal R_r=\{i:t_i\geq u_r\}$.
With the Breslow convention for ties,
$$
\ell_{\rm Cox}(\eta)
=\sum_r\left\{\sum_{i\in\mathcal D_r}\eta_i
       -d_r\log\sum_{i\in\mathcal R_r}e^{\eta_i}\right\}.
$$ {#eq-cox-pl}

This is the adopted survival estimation factor. It is not a normalized
joint density of event times. For untied events its conditional risk-set
interpretation motivates partial-likelihood inference; Breslow specifies
the tie approximation. Absolute survival probabilities would additionally
need an estimated baseline, for example
$\Delta\widehat H_0(u_r)=d_r/\sum_{i\in\mathcal R_r}e^{\widehat\eta_i}$.
The present target is relative risk, not absolute survival calibration.

## Ordinary and weighted estimation targets

Let $a_m>0$ be an omics-likelihood weight and $b\geq0$ a survival weight.
The generalized posterior kernel is
$$
\widetilde p(L,F,\beta\mid Y,t,\delta;\tau,g)
\ \propto\
\exp\left\{\sum_m a_m\ell_m+b\ell_{\rm Cox}(\eta)\right\}
\prod_{i,k}g_{L_k}(l_{ik})
\prod_{m,j,k}g_{F_{mk}}(f_{mjk})
\prod_k g_{\beta_k}(\beta_k).
$$ {#eq-kernel}

The ordinary observation-likelihood reference is $a_m=1$, $b=1$.
Even there the survival factor is a partial likelihood. Nonunit weights
define a power-likelihood or generalized-Bayes target, not the original
sampling likelihood. Weights are prespecified or tuned inside training;
there is no weight update in this document. Setting $b=0$ removes survival
from the *entire joint target*, including $\beta$; it does not reproduce
the no-feedback baseline, which still fits $\beta$.

Use the mean-field family
$$
q(L,F,\beta)=
\prod_{i,k}q(l_{ik})
\prod_{m,j,k}q(f_{mjk})
\prod_kq(\beta_k).
$$ {#eq-meanfield}

Define means $\bar l,\bar f,\bar\beta$, second moments
$l^{(2)},f^{(2)},\beta^{(2)}$, and variances
$v_l=l^{(2)}-\bar l^2$, $v_f=f^{(2)}-\bar f^2$,
$v_\beta=\beta^{(2)}-\bar\beta^2$. The second moments are not squared means.
The exact variational functional for the kernel is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal J(q,\tau,g)
={}&\sum_m a_m\E_q\ell_m+b\E_q\ell_{\rm Cox}(\eta)\\
&-\sum_{i,k}\KL(q(l_{ik})\Vert g_{L_k})\\
&-\sum_{m,j,k}\KL(q(f_{mjk})\Vert g_{F_{mk}})
 -\sum_k\KL(q(\beta_k)\Vert g_{\beta_k}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-objective}

For fixed hyperparameters it bounds the log normalizing constant of the
kernel. It is not automatically a bound on a full event-time marginal
likelihood. Empirical Bayes optimizes this functional over $g$ and $\tau$
as well as $q$. Mixed discrete/continuous priors require KL with respect
to the appropriate mixed measure; a Gaussian differential entropy alone
would omit the point mass.

The expectation of the Cox log-sum-exp has no general closed form.
The following updates optimize a stated quadratic surrogate. Keeping
that approximation visible is essential.

# Cox expansion and projection uncertainty {#sec-cox}

## Exact derivatives and the implemented working curvature

At an expansion point $\eta_0$, define the $n$-vector of risk-set
probabilities $P_r$ by
$$
(P_r)_i=
\frac{1\{i\in\mathcal R_r\}e^{\eta_{0i}}}
     {\sum_{h\in\mathcal R_r}e^{\eta_{0h}}}.
$$

Differentiating @eq-cox-pl gives
$$
u=\delta-\sum_r d_r P_r,\qquad
H=-\nabla^2\ell_{\rm Cox}(\eta_0)
 =\sum_r d_r\{\diag(P_r)-P_rP_r^\top\}.
$$ {#eq-cox-derivatives}

$H$ is positive semidefinite and generally dense. Its rows sum to zero,
reflecting invariance to a common shift in $\eta$. Its diagonal is
$\sum_r d_r(P_r)_i\{1-(P_r)_i\}$.

The current helper instead uses, before its numerical floor,
$$
W_{\rm work}=\diag\left(\sum_r d_r P_r\right).
$$ {#eq-working-curvature}

This omits the negative outer-product terms, including their diagonals.
At $\eta_0$, $W_{\rm work}-H=\sum_r d_rP_rP_r^\top$ is positive
semidefinite. This local relation does **not** establish a global
quadratic lower bound at all $\eta$. The implemented floor is $10^{-6}$
on each working weight; it is a numerical alteration, not part of the
exact Hessian.

## A common notation for the quadratic surrogate

For either $W=H$ or a stated working approximation, write
$$
Q(\eta;\eta_0,W)
=\ell_{\rm Cox}(\eta_0)
+u^\top(\eta-\eta_0)
-\tfrac12(\eta-\eta_0)^\top W(\eta-\eta_0).
$$ {#eq-quadratic}

Define
$$
t^\star=u+W\eta_0,\qquad
C_0=\ell_{\rm Cox}(\eta_0)-u^\top\eta_0
                    -\tfrac12\eta_0^\top W\eta_0.
$$
Then $Q=C_0+(t^\star)^\top\eta-\eta^\top W\eta/2$.
For diagonal positive $W$, the familiar working response is
$z^\star=\eta_0+W^{-1}u$, so $t^\star=Wz^\star$.
The $t^\star$ form also works with the singular full Hessian and avoids
an unnecessary matrix inverse.

Replace $\E\ell_{\rm Cox}$ in @eq-objective by $\E Q$ to obtain
$\mathcal J_Q$. The expansion point, $u$, and $W$ are held fixed during
an inner coordinate-ascent cycle. In particular, the linear coefficient
is $u+W\eta_0$, not just $u$.

## Moments of projected scores and the risk predictor

Let $\bar z_k=X\bar f_k$ and let $v_{f,ak}$ be the loading variance.
Mean-field independence of distinct loadings gives
$$
V_{z_k}=\Cov(z_k)=\sum_a v_{f,ak}x_ax_a^\top,\qquad
\E[z_kz_k^\top]=\bar z_k\bar z_k^\top+V_{z_k}.
$$ {#eq-score-moments}

Although individual loading posteriors are independent, different
subjects' projections are correlated: the same uncertain loadings are
used for every subject. Distinct factor columns are independent under
the chosen variational family. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_\eta&=\sum_k\bar\beta_k\bar z_k,\\
V_\eta&=\sum_k\left\{
  \beta_k^{(2)}V_{z_k}
  +v_{\beta,k}\bar z_k\bar z_k^\top\right\},\\
\E Q&=C_0+(t^\star)^\top\mu_\eta
-\tfrac12\mu_\eta^\top W\mu_\eta-\tfrac12\tr(WV_\eta).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-risk-moments}

At $\eta_0=\mu_\eta$, the last expression simplifies to
$\ell_{\rm Cox}(\mu_\eta)-\tr(WV_\eta)/2$.
After inner updates move $\mu_\eta$, the unsimplified expression must be
used until the expansion is refreshed. Mixing an old log partial
likelihood with updated means and dropping the linear correction
evaluates a different quantity.

For diagonal $W$, only $\Var(\eta_i)$ is needed, but the
$\beta_k^{(2)}V_{z_k}$ term remains. Dropping it is precisely the
fixed-projection approximation.

# Coordinate updates from the surrogate objective

## The normal-means reduction

For any scalar coordinate $\theta$ with prior $g$, suppose its expected
log-likelihood contribution, holding other variational factors fixed, is
$$
-\tfrac12 A\theta^2+B\theta+\mathrm{constant},\qquad A>0.
$$
The variational functional for this coordinate is the expectation of
this expression plus $\E_q\log g-\E_q\log q$. Taking its functional
derivative subject to $\int q=1$ yields
$$
\log q^\star(\theta)=\log g(\theta)-\tfrac12 A\theta^2+B\theta+C.
$$
Completing the square with $x=B/A$ and $s=A^{-1/2}$ gives
$$
q^\star(d\theta)=
\frac{\Normal(x;\theta,s^2)g(d\theta)}
     {\int\Normal(x;v,s^2)g(dv)}.
$$ {#eq-normal-means}

This establishes the EBNM interface; it is not a substitute for deriving
$A$ and $B$ for each parameter. The symbol $B$ here is a linear
coefficient in a quadratic, not the vector of survival coefficients.
Throughout this document the user's survival $B$ is denoted $\beta$.

## Shared subject scores $L$

For factor $k$, define the reconstruction residual excluding that
factor:
$$
\bar R_{mij}^{-k}
=y_{mij}-\sum_{h\ne k}\bar l_{ih}\bar f_{mjh}.
$$ {#eq-reconstruction-residual}

Holding the other coordinates fixed, expand the observation term:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&-\frac12\sum_{m,j}a_m\tau_{mj}
  \E_{-l_{ik}}\left[(R_{mij}^{-k}-l_{ik}f_{mjk})^2\right]\\
&\quad=-\frac12 l_{ik}^2
  \sum_{m,j}a_m\tau_{mj}f_{mjk}^{(2)}
 +l_{ik}\sum_{m,j}a_m\tau_{mj}
                 \bar R_{mij}^{-k}\bar f_{mjk}+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

The residual is independent of $f_{mjk}$ under mean field because it
excludes factor $k$. Under YFB, $\eta$ contains $F$ and $Y$, not $L$,
so there is no survival contribution to this coordinate. Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{L,ik}&=\sum_m a_m\sum_j\tau_{mj}f_{mjk}^{(2)},\\
B_{L,ik}&=\sum_m a_m\sum_j\tau_{mj}
                \bar R_{mij}^{-k}\bar f_{mjk}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-L-update}

The precision is the same across subjects with complete modalities.
Apply @eq-normal-means with $g_{L_k}$. An $n$-observation EBNM fit
per factor estimates its shared score prior. Return
$\bar l_{ik}=\E l_{ik}$ and $l_{ik}^{(2)}=\Var(l_{ik})+\bar l_{ik}^2$.
Compared with current YFB, the only structural change is the sum over
modalities, with explicit weights when used.

## Survival coefficients $\beta$

Define the mean contribution of all other factors to risk:
$$
\mu_{\eta,-k}=\sum_{h\ne k}\bar\beta_h\bar z_h,\qquad
h_k=t^\star-W\mu_{\eta,-k}.
$$ {#eq-survival-residual}

Insert $\eta=\eta_{-k}+\beta_kz_k$ into the quadratic. Terms depending
on $\beta_k$ are
$$
b\beta_k\bar z_k^\top h_k
-\frac b2\beta_k^2\E[z_k^\top Wz_k].
$$
The cross term factors because $\eta_{-k}$ and $z_k$ involve different
mean-field factor columns. By @eq-score-moments,
$$
\E[z_k^\top Wz_k]
=\bar z_k^\top W\bar z_k+\tr(WV_{z_k}).
$$
Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{\beta,k}
 &=b\left\{\bar z_k^\top W\bar z_k
                      +\sum_a v_{f,ak}x_a^\top Wx_a\right\},\\
B_{\beta,k}&=b\bar z_k^\top h_k.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-beta-update}

With a Normal prior variance $s_{\beta k}^2$, completing the square
including its precision gives
$$
v_{\beta,k}=(A_{\beta,k}+s_{\beta k}^{-2})^{-1},\quad
\bar\beta_k=v_{\beta,k}B_{\beta,k},\quad
\beta_k^{(2)}=v_{\beta,k}+\bar\beta_k^2.
$$ {#eq-beta-normal}

For a spike-and-slab alternative, use the posterior formula in
Section @sec-prior-fitting. The extra trace term in @eq-beta-update
is the loading-uncertainty correction missing from a fixed-projection
fit. For diagonal $W$ and $v_f=0$, these equations reduce to the
implemented beta-update algebra with $b=\mathrm{alpha}/\mathrm{beta\_divisor}$.

## Modality-specific loadings $F_m$

### Reconstruction contribution

For $a=(m,j)$ and factor $k$, expand
$$
\begin{aligned}
&-\frac{a_m\tau_{mj}}2
   \sum_i\E_{-f_{mjk}}(R_{mij}^{-k}-l_{ik}f_{mjk})^2\\
&\quad=-\frac12 A_{F,{\rm om},ak} f_{mjk}^2
       +B_{F,{\rm om},ak} f_{mjk}+C,
\end{aligned}
$$
where
$$
A_{F,{\rm om},ak}=a_m\tau_{mj}\sum_i l_{ik}^{(2)},\qquad
B_{F,{\rm om},ak}=a_m\tau_{mj}
                    \sum_i\bar l_{ik}\bar R_{mij}^{-k}.
$$ {#eq-F-omics}

Only this feature's modality appears in its reconstruction likelihood.
Its shared score column carries the information integrated from the
other modalities.

### Survival contribution, including same-factor features

Write
$$
z_k=x_a f_{ak}+z_{k,-a},\qquad
\bar z_{k,-a}=\bar z_k-x_a\bar f_{ak}.
$$
The factor-$k$ part of the expected survival quadratic is
$$
b\bar\beta_k\,\E[z_k]^\top h_k
-\frac b2\beta_k^{(2)}\E[z_k^\top Wz_k]+C.
$$
Expanding the second term while keeping the scalar $f_{ak}$ free gives
$$
\E_{-f_{ak}}[z_k^\top Wz_k]
= f_{ak}^2x_a^\top Wx_a
 +2f_{ak}x_a^\top W\bar z_{k,-a}+C.
$$
Consequently,
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{F,{\rm surv},ak}&=b\beta_k^{(2)}x_a^\top Wx_a,\\
B_{F,{\rm surv},ak}
 &=b\left\{\bar\beta_k x_a^\top h_k
          -\beta_k^{(2)}x_a^\top W\bar z_{k,-a}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-F-survival}

The second term in $B_{F,{\rm surv},ak}$ subtracts the contribution of
**all other features in the same factor**, including the other
modality. It has $\beta_k^{(2)}$, not $\bar\beta_k^2$, because the same
random coefficient multiplies both contributions. Removing factor $k$
from the working response is not enough to remove these interactions.
Even a diagonal $W$ does not make $X^\top WX$ diagonal.

Combine the two sources:
$$
A_{F,ak}=A_{F,{\rm om},ak}+A_{F,{\rm surv},ak},\qquad
B_{F,ak}=B_{F,{\rm om},ak}+B_{F,{\rm surv},ak}.
$$ {#eq-F-update}

Apply @eq-normal-means with the prior $g_{F_{mk}}$ belonging to this
modality and factor. The priors remain separate even though the
survival contributions couple their posterior updates.

### Consequence for implementation

In omics-only factorization, the feature updates within a factor are
conditionally separable, so one vectorized EBNM call can update a whole
loading block and estimate its prior. In joint YFB, $B_{F,ak}$ depends
on the current means of the other features. A simultaneous update using
stale values is a parallel fixed-point step, not an exact block
coordinate maximization.

A direct derivation-faithful algorithm therefore performs scalar
Gauss-Seidel posterior updates with the current modality prior fixed,
maintains $\bar z_k$ incrementally, and updates the prior parameters
using all features in that modality after a sweep. This is a
variational-EM procedure, not one independently re-fitted prior per
feature. A faster block or proximal method may later be designed, but
its objective and convergence behavior must be checked separately.

## Residual precisions $\tau_{mj}$

Independence of factor columns gives the variance-corrected residual
moment
$$
S_{mij}=
\left(y_{mij}-\sum_k\bar l_{ik}\bar f_{mjk}\right)^2
+\sum_k\left\{l_{ik}^{(2)}f_{mjk}^{(2)}
                         -\bar l_{ik}^2\bar f_{mjk}^2\right\}.
$$ {#eq-residual-moment}

To obtain it, expand the squared sum of factor products. Cross-factor
expectations equal products of means; the difference between the second
moment and the squared mean survives only within each factor. This
explains both the plus sign and the necessity of second moments.

The terms involving $\tau_{mj}$ are
$$
\frac{a_m n}{2}\log\tau_{mj}
-\frac{a_m\tau_{mj}}{2}\sum_i S_{mij}.
$$
Differentiate and set the result to zero:
$$
\frac{a_m n}{2\tau_{mj}}-\frac{a_m}{2}\sum_iS_{mij}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat\tau_{mj}=\frac n{\sum_iS_{mij}}.
$$ {#eq-tau-update}

The second derivative is negative for $a_m>0$. A constant modality
weight cancels from this point-estimation update; it does not cancel
from the score and loading posterior precisions. If a modality is
assigned weight zero, its residual precisions are not identified by
this objective. Positive weights are assumed throughout.

The existing denominator floor gives
$\tau_{mj}\leq1/\mathrm{tau\_floor}$ and should be described as a
constrained estimate. The multimodal method can reuse the algebra
blockwise without allocating all $S_m$ simultaneously. No
Gamma-prior, shape/rate update, or $q(\tau)$ is implied.

# Prior estimation and posterior moments {#sec-prior-fitting}

## Generic empirical-Bayes step

For a conditionally separable block with pseudo-data $(x_d,s_d)$,
optimizing its posterior factors and common prior jointly gives
$$
\widehat g=
\arg\max_{g\in\mathcal G}
\sum_d\log\left\{\int\Normal(x_d;\theta,s_d^2)g(d\theta)\right\}.
$$ {#eq-ebnm-marginal}

This follows by substituting the normalized posterior
@eq-normal-means into the block variational objective: the
posterior-versus-prior and pseudo-likelihood terms reduce to the log
normalizing integral. Apply this to $n$ subjects for $g_{L_k}$,
to $p_m$ features for $g_{F_{mk}}$ in the no-feedback case,
and to the scalar coefficient for $g_{\beta_k}$.

In coupled joint loading updates, the pseudo-data change when other
features change. Maximizing a product of marginal densities computed
from stale pseudo-data is not an exact joint loading-block update.
Instead alternate fixed-prior coordinate posteriors with the
fixed-posterior hyperparameter step
$$
\widehat g=\arg\max_g\sum_d\E_{q_d}\log g(\theta_d).
$$ {#eq-hyper-em}

The closed-form steps below implement this variational-EM option.
They also make every proposed hyperparameter estimable.

## Point-normal family

For prior $(1-\pi)\delta_0+\pi\Normal(0,s_0^2)$ and pseudo-likelihood
$x\mid\theta\sim\Normal(\theta,s^2)$, define
$$
d_0=\Normal(x;0,s^2),\quad
d_1=\Normal(x;0,s^2+s_0^2),\quad
r=\frac{\pi d_1}{(1-\pi)d_0+\pi d_1}.
$$
Conditional on being in the slab, completing the Gaussian square gives
$$
v=(s^{-2}+s_0^{-2})^{-1},\qquad \mu=vx/s^2.
$$
The posterior moments are
$$
\E\theta=r\mu,\qquad
\E\theta^2=r(v+\mu^2).
$$ {#eq-pn-moments}

Introduce a slab indicator $\gamma_d$. The expected complete-prior
log density for $N$ coordinates is, up to constants,
$$
\sum_d\{r_d\log\pi+(1-r_d)\log(1-\pi)\}
-\frac12\sum_d r_d\log s_0^2
-\frac{1}{2s_0^2}\sum_d\E\theta_d^2.
$$
Differentiating with respect to $\pi$ and $s_0^2$ yields
$$
\pi_{\rm new}=\frac1N\sum_d r_d,\qquad
s_{0,\rm new}^2=\frac{\sum_d\E\theta_d^2}{\sum_dr_d}.
$$ {#eq-pn-hyper}

The numerator is the unconditional second moment because the spike
contributes zero. These equations apply separately to each selected
modality-factor prior; no sum over the other modality appears.

## Point-exponential family

Use $(1-\pi)\delta_0+\pi r_0e^{-r_0\theta}1\{\theta\geq0\}$.
Multiplying the slab density by the normal pseudo-likelihood and
completing the square yields a Normal distribution truncated below at
zero with underlying mean
$\mu=x-r_0s^2$ and variance $s^2$.
Writing $h=\mu/s$ and $\lambda(h)=\phi(h)/\Phi(h)$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
d_1&=r_0\exp(-r_0x+r_0^2s^2/2)\Phi(h),\\
r&=\frac{\pi d_1}{(1-\pi)\Normal(x;0,s^2)+\pi d_1},\\
M_1&=\mu+s\lambda(h),\\
M_2&=\mu^2+s^2+\mu s\lambda(h),\\
\E\theta&=rM_1,\qquad \E\theta^2=rM_2.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pe-moments}

The slab integral $d_1$ follows by integrating the completed Normal
kernel from zero to infinity. The moment formulas follow from the
first two moments of that truncated Normal. Log-scale evaluation of
$d_1$, $\Phi$, and the inverse Mills ratio is needed in extreme tails;
the displayed expressions specify the mathematics, not a recommendation
to evaluate unstable exponentials directly.

The complete-prior expected log density contains
$$
\sum_d\{r_d\log\pi+(1-r_d)\log(1-\pi)\}
 +\left(\sum_dr_d\right)\log r_0-r_0\sum_d\E\theta_d.
$$
Setting its derivatives to zero gives
$$
\pi_{\rm new}=N^{-1}\sum_dr_d,\qquad
r_{0,\rm new}=\frac{\sum_dr_d}{\sum_d\E\theta_d}.
$$ {#eq-pe-hyper}

The score prior uses $N=n$; the loading prior uses $N=p_m$. This is
where modality-specific sparsity and amplitude are learned separately.

## Normal coefficient family and boundary cases

For a zero-centered Normal prior shared by a block of $N$ coefficients,
@eq-hyper-em gives $s_{\beta,\rm new}^2=N^{-1}\sum_d\E\beta_d^2$.
The implemented factor-specific baseline has $N=1$.
If optimizing the scalar normal-means marginal likelihood jointly
instead, differentiation of
$-\log(s^2+s_\beta^2)/2-x^2/\{2(s^2+s_\beta^2)\}$ gives
$$
\widehat s_\beta^2=\max(0,x^2-s^2).
$$
The direct marginal maximizer and one EM step are different operations;
repeated EM steps target the same stationary problem in this separable case.

If $\sum r_d=0$, the fitted prior is the point mass at zero and the
slab scale is unidentifiable. Do not divide zero by zero or report a
meaningful slab estimate. If $A=0$ and $B=0$, the likelihood supplies no
information and the fixed-prior posterior equals the prior. A precision
floor used for software compatibility is not evidence of information.
If all fitted factors vanish or the cohort has no events, the algorithm
must report that state rather than claim a prognostic model.
Boundary priors can be absorbing under EM, so initial priors should
start inside their admissible parameter space and multiple starts
should be considered after approval.

## Computing KL contributions correctly

For a posterior obtained from @eq-normal-means at fixed $g$,
let $m(x)=\int\Normal(x;\theta,s^2)g(d\theta)$. Then
$$
-\KL(q\Vert g)
=\log m(x)-\E_q\log\Normal(x;\theta,s^2),
$$
where
$$
\E_q\log\Normal(x;\theta,s^2)
=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi s^2)
-\frac{x^2-2x\E\theta+\E\theta^2}{2s^2}.
$$ {#eq-kl}

This is the identity used by compute_ebnm_kl. The sum over loading
blocks must retain every modality's term. After a hyperparameter update
changes $g$ while holding $q$ fixed, an old EBNM normalizing constant
cannot be used unchanged. Evaluate the mixed-distribution KL directly,
or add $\E_q\log(g_{\rm new}/g_{\rm old})$ to the stored negative KL.
Likewise, never recompute pseudo-data and combine their likelihood
normalizer with posterior moments from a different update.

# Dimensional imbalance: what separate priors can and cannot do

## Ordinary likelihood first

With $a_m=1$, a modality contributes more independent observations when
it has more features. Its contribution to score precision is
$$
A_{L,k}^{(m)}=\sum_{j=1}^{p_m}\tau_{mj}f_{mjk}^{(2)}.
$$
If those expected precision-weighted second moments have comparable
means across modalities, $A_{L,k}^{(m)}$ grows with $p_m$. This is a
likelihood property, not a consequence of mistakenly sharing the priors.
Separate $g_{F_{mk}}$ can learn different sparsity and amplitude, and
feature-wise $\tau_{mj}$ can reflect different residual variances.
Neither guarantees cancellation of the feature-count effect.

Consider a representative loading prior with nonzero probability $\pi_m$.
Its second moment is $\pi_m s_m^2$ for point-normal and $2\pi_m/r_m^2$
for point-exponential. At comparable residual precision, a rough prior
scale for a modality's contribution is therefore proportional to
$p_m\pi_m s_m^2$ or $2p_m\pi_m/r_m^2$. This is an explanatory scale
calculation, not the posterior update. Balancing those quantities would
require an explicit constraint or hyperprior; independent EB fitting
does not impose one.

## Explicit likelihood-weight alternatives

Three choices illustrate the distinction:

| Formulation | Omics weights | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Ordinary reference | $a_m=1$ | Every measured feature contributes its ordinary likelihood |
| Per-feature average | $a_m=1/p_m$ | Each modality contributes its mean feature log-likelihood |
| Equal effective counts | $a_m=p_{\rm ref}/p_m$ | Equal feature-count scale with an explicit reference count |

The latter two have the same *relative* modality weights but different
absolute evidence strength relative to priors, entropy, and the survival
term. The reference $p_{\rm ref}$ is an additional declared constant;
it must not be chosen implicitly.

More generally one can write $a_m=\rho_m/p_m$ with fixed positive
$\rho_m$. If the earlier alpha convention is desired, explicitly define
$a_m=(1-\alpha)\rho_m/p_m$ and $b=\alpha/s_T$ with a declared survival
scale $s_T$. This changes every relevant update, not only the reported
objective. The ordinary reference is easier to express directly by
$a_m=b=1$; it is not equivalent to alpha = 0.5 when prior/entropy terms
are left unchanged.

In the pure-reconstruction loading update, $a_m$ cancels from $x=B/A$
but changes $s=A^{-1/2}$. Consequently it changes shrinkage and the
fitted prior. In $L$, relative modality weights change both $x$ and $s$.
In joint $F$, cancellation generally fails because survival contributes
additional terms. In $\tau$, the weight cancels as shown above.

The loading prior/entropy contribution still contains $p_m$ terms.
Weighting the observation likelihood alone is therefore not a theorem
of equal posterior modality influence. If one also weights loading KL
terms, the coordinate posterior and hyperparameter objective change
again; that is a different functional and is not adopted here.
Multiplying the **entire** objective by a common positive constant
leaves its maximizer unchanged. Multiplying only likelihood terms does
not.

## Informative, null, duplicate, and rescaled features

**Additional informative features.** Under conditional independence they
can improve estimation of shared scores. Removing all benefit of extra
informative measurements is not necessarily desirable. Evaluate whether
the larger block contributes independent signal or redundant evidence.

**Additional null features.** An adaptive loading prior can shrink their
means, but posterior second moments can remain positive. Their aggregate
precision contribution and the fitted noise levels should be inspected.
A large CpG block must not be assumed harmless merely because most
posterior means are small.

**Duplicated features.** If one modality's features and loading moments
are repeated $r$ times, its unweighted score precision and signal
multiply by $r$. With weights divided by $r$, these particular sums are
unchanged. The full fit need not be invariant: there are now more prior
terms and correlated residuals, and YFB projection contributions also
duplicate unless separately adjusted. This is a useful diagnostic of
pseudoreplication, not an exact invariance requirement for the entire
weighted model.

**Measurement rescaling.** Under $Y_m'=d_mY_m$,
$F_m'=d_mF_m$, and $\tau_m'=\tau_m/d_m^2$, the Gaussian model transforms
consistently, with the usual data-density Jacobian. Raw YFB projections
instead satisfy $Y_m'F_m'=d_m^2Y_mF_m$. Thus noise adjustment alone does
not make YFB prediction scale-invariant. Modality preprocessing and
projection normalization need their own specification.

The initial scientific comparison should keep the ordinary likelihood,
fit separate priors, and examine these contributions. Weighted targets
are explicit alternatives if the resulting domination reflects unwanted
feature-count or redundancy effects. The comparison must use training
data; the independent cohort cannot decide the weights.

# Projection normalization, support, and identifiability

## Three projection definitions

For a point estimate of the loading columns, compare
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{raw:}\quad z_k
 &=\sum_m c_mY_m f_{mk},\\
\text{global norm:}\quad z_k
 &=\frac{\sum_mY_m f_{mk}}
           {\sqrt{\sum_m\|f_{mk}\|^2}},\\
\text{per-modality norm:}\quad z_k
 &=\sum_m c_mY_m\frac{f_{mk}}{\|f_{mk}\|}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-normalization-comparison}

The first is the linear model derived in full above. The second matches
the structure of current YFB prediction, apart from its numerical
epsilon. The third gives each modality its own unit-norm loading
direction; it is an alternative for review, not a guaranteed balance of
projected variance. Correlation and variance within $Y_m$ still matter.
It can also amplify a very weak nonzero loading block, making the
zero-block convention particularly consequential.

Current YFB normalizes the **posterior mean** loading, not every draw of
$F$. In general,
$\E[F/\|F\|]\ne\E[F]/\|\E[F]\|$. Treating a normalized mean projection as
fixed during $\beta$ fitting is a plug-in approximation. It must not be
substituted for a stochastic normalized projection in a joint posterior
without stating that change.

## Derivatives for a normalized loading direction

For one column write $r=(f^\top f+\epsilon)^{1/2}$ and
$z=Xf/r$. The current epsilon is a numerical regularizer; with
$\epsilon>0$ it changes exact scale invariance. For coordinate $f_a$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial z}{\partial f_a}
 &=\frac{x_a}{r}-\frac{(Xf)f_a}{r^3},\\
\frac{\partial^2z}{\partial f_a^2}
 &=-\frac{2x_af_a}{r^3}-\frac{Xf}{r^3}
                         +\frac{3(Xf)f_a^2}{r^5}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-normalized-derivatives}

These follow from $\partial r/\partial f_a=f_a/r$ and the product rule.
For per-modality normalization the same equations apply within each
block, multiplied by $c_m$; for global normalization the norm uses all
modalities, so even its denominator couples the blocks.

For a point coefficient $\beta_k$, the survival gradient for $f_a$ is
$(\partial\eta/\partial f_a)^\top u$. Its second derivative is
$$
-\left(\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial f_a}\right)^\top
 H\left(\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial f_a}\right)
+u^\top\frac{\partial^2\eta}{\partial f_a^2}.
$$
The second term is absent from a linear projection. It can change
concavity. Replacing $x_a$ by $x_a/r$ in the raw update and ignoring
the derivatives of $r$ does not derive the normalized model.

## Estimation implications for normalized alternatives

For a stochastic normalized predictor, the exact coordinate equation is
$$
q^\star(f_a)\ \propto\
g(f_a)\exp\left\{-\tfrac12A_{\rm om}f_a^2+B_{\rm om}f_a
 +b\,\E_{-f_a}\ell_{\rm Cox}(\eta(f_a,F_{-a},\beta))\right\}.
$$ {#eq-normalized-coordinate}

The Cox term can instead be replaced by $Q$ for a stated surrogate, but
its composition with the normalization remains nonquadratic.
$L$ and $\tau$ retain their reconstruction updates. For $\beta$ under
a quadratic Cox surrogate, @eq-beta-update still holds with
$\bar z_k=\E z_k$ and $V_{z_k}=\Cov(z_k)$ computed for the chosen nonlinear
map; @eq-score-moments is no longer valid. Prior hyperparameter EM steps
retain their form once coordinate responsibilities and moments are known.

A numerical implementation of this alternative would integrate the
continuous slab and point mass separately for each coordinate, normalize
their masses, and integrate their first two moments. Inner expectations
over other coordinates require quadrature in tiny checks and controlled
Monte Carlo at realistic dimensions. Numerical integration error and
Monte Carlo error must be reported. This is substantially more expensive
than the linear surrogate algorithm and is not a drop-in EBNM call.
A local linearization is a possible cheaper approximation, but requires
the Jacobian in @eq-normalized-derivatives and its own objective checks.

With $\epsilon=0$, a spike-and-slab prior gives positive probability to
an all-zero loading block, where the normalized map is undefined.
One must specify its projection as zero at that atom; this yields a
discontinuity near zero. Alternatively $\epsilon>0$ gives a smooth map
everywhere with an explicitly scale-dependent regularization. These
alternatives are shown for advisor choice, not resolved by silently
inserting a floor.

## Nonnegative support and expression--methylation association

Nonnegative score and loading priors imply a nonnegative reconstructed
mean $LF_m^\top$. Gaussian noise can be negative, but this does not make
that mean family capable of representing arbitrary centered positive
and negative signal. Centered expression or methylation M-values and
nonnegative priors must therefore be considered together.

Within a single factor, nonnegative loadings in both modalities move
in the same direction as its score. They cannot represent opposite
directions for that one factor. Multiple complementary factors may
produce inverse associations in a fitted dataset, but that is not the
same model as a single signed shared effect. With independent
nonnegative score priors, the prior marginal cross-feature covariance
from shared factors is nonnegative.

Methylation associations depend on genomic context. A primary study
reported negative effects enriched near transcription start sites and
positive effects enriched in gene bodies
([Nature Communications, 2022](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-35196-3)).
The model should not assume a universal inverse association or reverse
all CpGs.

Three analysis-scale choices deserve review: retain nonnegative
transformed measurements and acknowledge their baseline structure;
use signed loading and possibly signed score priors for centered
measurements; or extend the model with feature intercepts. Intercepts
are **not** part of the core parameterization. If selected, define
$y_{mij}=\mu_{mj}+\sum_kl_{ik}f_{mjk}+e_{mij}$ and, at fixed moments,
differentiate the Gaussian residual sum of squares to obtain
$$
\widehat\mu_{mj}=\frac1n\sum_i
 \left(y_{mij}-\sum_k\bar l_{ik}\bar f_{mjk}\right).
$$
The core updates then use $Y_m-\mu_m$. Score-location constraints and
whether the survival projection also uses this centered matrix would
need to be specified together. Adding this parameter is an advisor
decision, not an undocumented preprocessing substitution.

## Scale, sign, permutation, and factor number

For linear YFB, the simultaneous transformation
$$
l_k'=d_kl_k,\quad f_{mk}'=f_{mk}/d_k,\quad
\beta_k'=d_k\beta_k,\qquad d_k>0
$$ {#eq-gauge}
preserves reconstruction and $\eta$. If prior scales are learned,
transform them too: $r_{Lk}'=r_{Lk}/d_k$,
$r_{Fmk}'=d_kr_{Fmk}$, and
$s_{\beta k}'=d_ks_{\beta k}$. The scale ambiguity is not resolved
merely by independent scale-adaptive priors.

A reporting convention for a nonzero factor can set
$n^{-1}\sum_i l_{ik}^{(2)}=1$ using
$d_k=(n^{-1}\sum_i l_{ik}^{(2)})^{-1/2}$. Transform second moments by
$d_k^2$ for $L,\beta$ and by $d_k^{-2}$ for $F_m$, and transform the
prior parameters consistently. This is a change of coordinates, not
rescaling data. It must not be applied using these same beta rules to
the normalized-projection model, where the invariances differ.

Factor permutations always remain. Signed priors permit sign changes
with corresponding coefficient/score transformations. General
invertible rotations preserve $LF^\top$ but need not preserve
independent sparse priors, mean-field distributions, or their objective.
Do not enforce orthogonality post hoc and claim the posterior is unchanged.

Report subspace recovery as well as matched-factor recovery. A
factor-matching procedure must handle permutation and applicable scale
and sign transformations. Keep separate summaries of omics activity,
activity in each modality, and prognostic activity; a small beta is not
the definition of an absent omics factor. The existing real-data
$K_{\rm init}=7$ and activity thresholds are not validated multimodal
defaults. Numerical $K$ choices remain for the later simulation design.

# Algorithms and compatibility

## A direct multimodal version of current no-feedback YFB

The closest adaptation preserves the present learning direction:

1. Fit shared $L$, separate $F_m$ priors, and feature-wise $\tau_m$ using
   the omics objective. The ordinary baseline sets $a_m=1$.
2. Form $\widehat Z$ from the stacked posterior mean loadings using the
   current global column normalization.
3. Fit $\beta$ on those fixed projections with the current Cox working
   curvature and alpha scaling. This can be interleaved with omics
   iterations for compatibility, but final coefficients must be
   converged against the final saved projection.
4. Save projection norms, feature order, fitted priors, transformations,
   and any training-only orientation choice for external prediction.

This is an omics representation plus a conditional survival model.
Its objectives are an omics variational objective and a conditional Cox
coefficient objective, reported separately. There is no feedback path
from survival to the representation. It is not obtained by setting
$b=0$ in the joint target.

When $M=1$, with the same preprocessing, priors, initialization,
update order, floors, and finalization, its algebra reduces to current
YFB. The joint uncertainty-aware model need not reproduce that fit:
those are different estimation procedures.

## Joint linear-projection variational algorithm

This is the derivation-complete reference algorithm for the raw or
fixed-weight linear projection. It uses the full $H$ or the explicitly
declared working $W$; comparison of these approximations is left to review.

1. **Initialize from training omics.** Use nonzero factor columns and
   interior prior parameters. Adapt the existing SVD initialization for
   the selected support; retain initialization provenance. A
   reconstruction warm start followed by a coefficient fit can reduce
   early factor collapse. No validation outcomes are consulted.
2. **Set an outer expansion.** Compute all current moments, $\eta_0$,
   the Cox score, and $W$. Store $t^\star$ and $C_0$.
3. **Perform inner coordinate sweeps.** For each factor, update $\beta_k$,
   the shared $L_k$, and loading coordinates across modalities using
   @eq-beta-update, @eq-L-update, and @eq-F-update. Hold the Cox expansion
   fixed; update residuals and projected means after each changed
   coordinate.
4. **Update priors.** Use blockwise EBNM where conditionally separable.
   For joint loading priors use the fixed-posterior EM steps after
   fixed-prior scalar sweeps. Compute KL consistently with the current
   posterior and prior.
5. **Update noise and evaluate.** Apply @eq-tau-update to each block and
   evaluate $\mathcal J_Q$ using @eq-risk-moments and all KL terms.
   An exact inner update must not decrease this *fixed-expansion*
   functional beyond numerical tolerance. A decrease requires diagnosis.
6. **Refresh and monitor.** After inner convergence, refresh the Cox
   expansion. Monitor coefficient, score, loading, precision, and
   objective changes, not just training C-index. Record separate
   reconstruction, Cox, uncertainty, and prior contributions.
7. **Finalize coherently.** Recompute risk projections and all
   diagnostics from the saved final state. Apply only approved
   parameterization conventions. Retain nonconvergence, degenerate
   factors, and boundary priors as explicit diagnostics.

Changing the local expansion can change $\mathcal J_Q$ without
monotonicity in the exact $\mathcal J$. A quadratic Taylor approximation
is not a global lower bound, and inner coordinate ascent does not prove
outer convergence. For development, approximate $\E\ell_{\rm Cox}$ with
posterior draws and record Monte Carlo uncertainty. Such monitoring
can detect failures; it does not turn a local approximation into a
theorem. Damping or a proven bound is a later inference choice if
outer instability persists. Do not silently fall back to alpha_F = 0
and report joint-model convergence.

## What can be reused

The residual-moment algebra, Normal conjugacy, scalar normal-means
posterior machinery, Cox risk-set construction, and most parameter
names can be reused. A loading-prior identifier must become a
modality-indexed object. $L$ and $\beta$ remain shared.

The shared score update must aggregate modality contributions. Loading
updates require per-modality priors; joint loading updates additionally
require the same-factor interaction correction. The joint coefficient
and objective calculations require projection uncertainty. Reusing the
old combined ELBO monitor unchanged would conceal differences in
objective weights and uncertainty.

For the mathematical no-feedback reduction, remove the survival terms
from $F$ *and* treat projections as fixed for coefficient fitting.
For the omics-only reduction of the joint model, set $b=0$; then
$q(\beta)=g_\beta$. These are distinct checks.

# Independent validation and future cohort compatibility

## Frozen training-to-validation map

Let validation data be $Y_m^{\rm val}$ with $n_{\rm val}$ rows.
Modality names and within-modality feature identifiers must match the
training contract. Reorder subjects by verified identifiers before
fitting or prediction, never by row position alone. Validation subjects
may be reordered freely provided both modality blocks follow the same
permutation.

Feature selection, imputation rules if later approved, transformation
parameters, centering/scaling, projection weights, fitted priors,
loadings, beta, and factor-retention rules are learned or fixed using
training data. Outcome-independent assay QC may operate on validation
measurements, but it must not refit the statistical prediction map.
All tuning and CV preprocessing must be repeated inside each training
fold rather than learned once on the full training cohort.

For the linear projection, the frozen plug-in risk prediction is
$$
\widehat\eta^{\rm val}
=\sum_k\bar\beta_k\sum_m c_mY_m^{\rm val}\bar f_{mk}.
$$ {#eq-validation}

For the compatibility model, substitute
$\bar f_{mk}/D_{kk}^{\rm train}$ using the saved global training norm.
For other approved normalization rules, apply their corresponding
frozen training quantities. Normalizing on the validation cohort or
refitting beta would change the prediction rule.

Under mean-field joint inference with a linear projection, the
plug-in expression is the posterior mean risk predictor. Uncertainty
can be propagated by applying @eq-risk-moments with the validation
design matrix, without validation outcomes. For stochastic normalized
models, posterior-mean prediction instead requires integration through
the nonlinear map; normalization of posterior means is an additional
approximation.

Missing required modalities or features are not silently imputed by
zero and norms are not recomputed on an arbitrary feature subset.
For the initial complete-data design, incompatible inputs must stop.
An assay-based common feature universe may be prespecified from
platform metadata; outcome- or value-dependent feature selection uses
training only. If complete matching is impossible, a missing-feature
extension must be reviewed before reporting validation results.

## Latent scores for reconstruction are a separate output

To evaluate validation reconstruction, hold $F_m,\tau_m,g_{L_k}$
fixed at training estimates and infer validation score distributions
using @eq-L-update with validation omics only. Iterate the score
coordinates; do not re-estimate the score priors on validation.
This produces $\bar L^{\rm val}$ for reconstruction, not the YFB
survival covariates.

A point-estimate Gaussian alternative without prior shrinkage solves
$$
\widehat L^{\rm val}=
\left\{\sum_m a_mY_m^{\rm val}\diag(\tau_m)\bar F_m\right\}
\left\{\sum_m a_m\bar F_m^\top\diag(\tau_m)\bar F_m\right\}^{+}.
$$
The pseudoinverse handles rank deficiency. This is weighted least
squares conditional on fixed mean loadings, not the same posterior
inference as the moment-based score update. It is supplied only to
clarify the distinction from the existing LB prediction routine.

Evaluate survival outcomes only after predictions are frozen. Report
discrimination and uncertainty alongside convergence and factor
activity. Do not use validation concordance to flip the sign of beta.
A factor reorientation that preserves $\eta$ is harmless; negating
beta alone changes the statistical fit and is not a joint-objective
update. The current training-concordance sign correction belongs to
the compatibility baseline and should be reported if used.

## Cohorts are orthogonal to modality partitions

If multiple training cohorts are later included, the observation model
can be extended to
$$
Y_m=LF_m^\top+C A_m^\top+E_m,
$$
where $C$ is an observed $n\times(C_{\rm train}-1)$ corner-point
cohort-indicator matrix and $A_m$ contains feature-specific offsets.
These indicator columns are not biological factors and their survival
coefficients are zero in the existing offset extension. Their Gaussian
prior updates use the same feature precision and, in a weighted
objective, the same modality likelihood weight.

Stratified survival instead sums @eq-cox-pl over training strata and
modifies the risk sets. Cohort-specific beta instead replaces
$\beta_k$ by $\beta_k^{c(i)}$ with an explicitly chosen pooling prior.
None of these mechanisms partitions $F$ by modality. With one
training cohort they are absent; an unseen validation cohort does not
supply an estimable new offset or beta without changing the validation
design. A full combined-cohort derivation is future work.

# Translation to implementation and simulation after review

## Minimal interface changes

A future fit should accept a named list of numeric matrices, one
per modality, plus survival vectors keyed to verified subject IDs.
The fitted object should retain shared EL/EL2 and EBeta/EBeta2 and
modality-indexed EF/EF2, Tau, prior fits, feature IDs, and training
preprocessing/projection metadata. Existing single-matrix callers
should continue to work through their existing path. No such API
has been implemented in this deliverable.

Loading-prior arguments must be separate from the shared score prior.
The old prior_LF convenience setting can remain an explicit baseline
mapping, but it must not cause features from different modalities to
be passed into the same fitted loading prior.
Likelihood weights, projection coefficients, and objective type need
distinct names and saved values; alpha_F must not be overloaded to
mean modality balance.

## Computation at CpG scale

At $p_1=20{,}000$ and $p_2=400{,}000$, a dense $p\times p$ double
matrix alone would require about $1.41$ TB in decimal units.
It must not be constructed. A dense $n\times p$ data matrix requires
$8np$ bytes (about $1.68$ GB at $n=500$), before residuals, copies,
second moments, and temporary products. These are illustrative memory
calculations, not selected simulation sample sizes.

Keep modality blocks separate. For diagonal $W$, scalar loading
updates and variance traces need products such as
$x_a^\top Wx_a$ and $x_a^\top W\bar z_{k,-a}$, which can be computed
without $X^\top WX$. Updating $\bar z_k$ after one loading change costs
$O(n)$. Dense diagonal-working-curvature sweeps cost roughly
$O(nK\sum_mp_m)$, apart from EBNM optimization. Full-Hessian products
can be more expensive; use risk-set products or a declared
approximation and benchmark them. Scalar R-to-package calls per CpG
may be a practical bottleneck even without a memory problem.

The exact Gauss-Seidel loading updates are sequential through their
shared projections. Parallelizing them naively changes the algorithm.
Independent simulation seeds and training folds are safer first
parallelization targets. If later run on Longleaf, request memory
based on measured peak allocation, control BLAS threads inside SLURM
workers, and avoid nested parallel oversubscription.

## Synthetic data: mechanism before scenario grid

Generate training and validation subjects independently conditional
on common population parameters $F_m,\tau_m,\beta$ and score-prior
distributions. Sharing these parameters is what permits evaluation
of generalization to new subjects. Independently resampling the
validation loading matrix would instead test a changed population and
must be labeled a distribution-shift scenario.

For a well-specified YFB experiment, first generate $L$, then $Y_m$,
then survival using the selected YFB projection of the realized $Y_m$.
The existing multi-cohort simulation uses an $L\beta$ survival
mechanism; reusing it without modification would be a misspecification
experiment. Include an $L\beta$ mechanism only as an explicitly named
robustness comparison.

Candidate scenario dimensions are modality feature-count ratio,
sparsity, residual precision, feature redundancy, complementary versus
redundant modality signal, nonnegative versus signed true loadings,
and factors absent from one modality. Start with small dimensions
that preserve the expression-to-CpG ratio, then measure scaling before
full-size runs. Exact sample sizes, effect sizes, repetitions,
censoring fractions, and factor numbers are intentionally deferred
until model review; do not copy the current gene-expression defaults
as if validated for multimodal data.

Candidate estimands include shared subspace recovery, matched
loading recovery by modality, reconstruction error by modality,
survival discrimination on untouched validation data, activity
classification, runtime, memory, and convergence/failure rates.
Compare expression-only, methylation-only, direct no-feedback
multimodal YFB, and the approved joint model using comparable tuning
budgets. Assess integration benefit against both single-modality
models; report uncertainty over independently generated replicates.

## Real-data preprocessing decisions

The real-data design needs modality-specific assay QC, sample identity
checks, feature annotation/version matching, and a frozen
training-to-validation transformation. Expression counts may require
a library-size-aware transform; methylation proportions may be kept
on a bounded measurement scale or transformed to M-values for a
Gaussian working likelihood. These choices have different support
implications under nonnegative priors. They remain for review with
the actual assays and are not implemented by this mathematical note.

Investigate CpG redundancy and batch/platform shifts separately from
feature-count balance. Matched subjects do not eliminate assay effects.
Do not infer a one-to-one gene--CpG correspondence or a universal
inverse relation during feature matching.

# Verification and advisor decisions

## Reproducible numerical checks

The companion check script validates the algebra on small deterministic
examples; it does not fit or simulate a proposed multimodal model.
Its examples use nonzero posterior variances and correlated features
across modalities so that dropping the interaction or uncertainty
terms produces detectable errors.

```{r}
#| label: derivation-checks
#| results: asis
source("verify_derivation.R", local = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("**Verification result:** %d of %d checks passed.\n\n",
            sum(check_results$passed), nrow(check_results)))
knitr::kable(check_results[, c("check", "passed")],
             col.names = c("Algebra or behavior checked", "Passed"),
             row.names = FALSE)
```

The checks cover exact Breslow derivatives with tied events;
the implemented working-curvature relation; finite-difference
derivatives of the expected quadratic for $L,F,\beta,\tau$;
enumerated risk moments; prior posterior moments and hyperparameter
stationarity; modality-partition reduction; weighted duplication sums;
and normalized-projection derivatives.

These checks verify local formulas, not convergence or predictive
performance of a future implementation. No numerical fit comparison
is claimed. After code implementation, run the repository test suite
and add end-to-end tests for subject/feature alignment, frozen
prediction, separate prior fitting, objective accounting, and
the matched single-modality reduction.

## Decisions to take to the advisors

| Decision | Starting point | Alternative or required resolution |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Representation | One shared $L$; separate $F_m$ priors | Allow a block to shrink to zero; already agreed |
| Data structure | One matched training cohort and one matched validation cohort | Multiple training cohorts deferred |
| Observation model | Gaussian working likelihood; feature-wise precision MLE | Confirm transforms and residual adequacy |
| Loading support | Nonnegative point-exponential | Compare signed loadings and centered-data compatibility |
| Evidence balance | Ordinary observation likelihood first | Explicit modality weights if justified |
| Projection | Current normalized mean projection for compatibility | Linear joint reference versus nonlinear normalized joint model |
| Supervision | Joint survival-informed $F$ derivation | Retain no-feedback YFB as the direct implementation baseline |
| Inference | Coordinate updates for a declared Cox surrogate | Select working versus exact curvature and stability strategy |
| Beta prior | Existing zero-centered Normal per factor | Pooling or sparse alternative requires separate choice |
| Validation | Frozen training map; outcomes only for evaluation | Missing-feature or cohort adaptation needs a new protocol |

The main dependency is projection choice: it determines whether
normal-means coordinate updates remain available. Weighting and prior
support must then be assessed on that same parameterization and
analysis scale. This document supplies the mathematical alternatives;
it does not approve one by implication.

## Build, provenance, and teach-back

From the repository root:

```bash
Rscript derivations/multimodal_YFB/verify_derivation.R
quarto render derivations/multimodal_YFB/multimodal_YFB_derivation.qmd --to pdf
```

Rendering executes the verification script and stops on a failed
assertion. The source remains editable alongside the PDF. The
standalone check script uses base R; rendering additionally needs
Quarto, knitr, and a working LaTeX installation. It does not source
the production fitting scripts or load real data.

The mathematical document's input is the existing YFB parameterization
and the agreed matched-modality design; its output is a set of
explicit estimation objectives and derived update procedures.
The main design choice is to separate direct compatibility from
joint inference so that new modality priors do not conceal changes
in survival supervision. The main limitation is that a local Cox
surrogate and a mean-field approximation do not establish global
convergence or calibrated uncertainty.

The check script's input is small deterministic numerical fixtures.
It compares derivatives, exact finite-support expectations, and
numerical integrals with the equations. Its output is a named table
of assertions; any failure terminates execution. These computations
test mathematical identities rather than performance of an
unimplemented model.

# Sources and local references

The update algebra in this note is derived explicitly above. The
following sources establish the empirical-Bayes framework and
software conventions; they are not substitutes for the derivation.

- Wang and Stephens (2021), [Empirical Bayes Matrix Factorization](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-589.html).
  Background on learning factor/loading priors with variational empirical Bayes.
- Willwerscheid, Carbonetto, and Stephens (2025),
  [ebnm: An R Package for Solving the Empirical Bayes Normal Means Problem Using a Variety of Prior Families](https://www.jstatsoft.org/index.php/jss/article/view/v114i03).
  Background on normal-means prior estimation.
- [Official ebnm reference](https://stephenslab.github.io/ebnm/reference/ebnm.html).
  Fixed prior mode, prior scale conventions, fixed-prior posterior calls,
  and posterior moment outputs. Local package version inspected: 1.1.42.
- [Quantifying the role of transcript levels in mediating DNA methylation effects on complex traits and diseases](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-35196-3)
  (Nature Communications, 2022). Biological context for the sign comparison.
- Local mathematical references: \path{derivations/cox_on_YF/} and
  \path{docs/notes/YFB_update_derivations_detailed_05_08_26.qmd}.
  These describe earlier YFB formulas; the audit in Section 2
  identifies where they cannot be carried over unchanged.
- Local implementation references: \path{code/fit_cox_on_yf.R};
  \path{code/update_L_surv_YFB.R}; \path{code/update_F_surv_YFB.R};
  \path{code/update_beta.R}; \path{code/update_tau.R};
  \path{code/compute_elbo.R}; \path{code/predict_cox_on_yf.R}.
- Cohort references: \path{code/update_F_cohort.R} and
  \path{code/update_beta_cohort.R}; stratified risk-set handling in
  \path{code/fit_cox_on_yf.R}.
